newsitem.title: KENYA: In the chaos of the Great Lakes, some still smile.
newsitem.headline: In the chaos of the Great Lakes, some still smile.

text.p: Conflict in Zaire will have mixed effects on East Africa, threatening economic disruption through an influx of refugees and arms but also bringing more aid dollars into the region, economic analysts said on Tuesday.
No politician would dream of welcoming the latest crisis and, with so many dangers looming from the unpredictability of a volatile situation, few would obviously stand to gain.
"Conflict in eastern Zaire poses a serious threat to the stability of the entire region," Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi told a crisis meeting of regional leaders in Nairobi.

Some businessmen fear the crisis has the potential to cause major economic disruption through cut trade routes and an influx of refugees -- for example into Uganda's prime coffee-growing area -- at a time when East Africa was getting its political and economic act together.

But regional chaos could also bring certain economic benefits, as clan-based fighting which erupted next-door in Somalia did for Kenya and ethnic bloodshed in Rwanda and Burundi in 1993-4 for Uganda, political analysts said.

Economists said fighting in eastern Zaire meant dollars from international agencies would continue to flow into the two most stable states in the region, which aid groups use as main logistics bases for relief efforts in Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire.
"One of the things that help prop up Kenya's exchange rate is the flow of money from aid workers," David Icharia, of Coopers and Lybrand consultants, told Reuters.
He also saw Uganda's shilling supported in the same way.

Coffee traders said new tensions in the Bukavu and Goma cities of Zaire also meant that coffee supplies from that area could in the long term be tight and, coupled with sanctions on Burundi, prices would rise for Kenya and Ugandan arabicas.
The region's troubles this decades do not seem to have had a negative impact on one of Kenya's main money-spinners, tourism.
Until fighting flared in eastern Zaire, Rwanda had been coaxing tourists back to see its unique mountain gorillas but this small source of income has dried up, for now.
An emerging markets expert at a leading merchant bank said the last five years had shown regional crises could have a silver lining for some.
"When Kenya was in trouble with Western donors in 1991, relief agencies supplied the dollars that kept it afloat," he said.

"You must understand that after the fighting (in Somalia), in economic terms, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania made no losses. In fact, it does not matter to these countries whether another state is hived off from Zaire," he said.
However, available dollars are far from the whole picture.
Tanzania houses some 600,000 refugees from Rwanda and Burundi, Somalian refugees have made Kenya home and now some 20,000 Zaireans have joined Sudanese refugees in Uganda.

"Refugees are not a good influence. They are a burden on the resources of host countries and clearly undermine economic development," said one official from the secretariat of East African Cooperation, that groups Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.
"You do not want a situation where fighting means refugees will think your country is part of their own, that they are entitled to your food and to your jobs."
Moi and other Kenyan leaders have repeatedly blamed refugees for rising crime in the nation.
They say guns have illegally filtered in from Somalia and Rwandans have extended their feud to Kenya, bringing in guns.
A new U.N. report says Kenya has become the regional centre for gun-running to Hutu rebels from Burundi and Rwanda.
Across Kenya and Uganda, wealthier refugees and aid workers are blamed for boosting housing costs as they rent homes in prime districts at prices well above what locals can afford.
